Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment
Additional Titles
Budget Stabilization Account Cap Increase and Gann Limit Changes Amendment
Rainy day Fund
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email) The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting. It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codesTOCSelected.xhtml?tocCode=CONS&tocTitle=+California+Constitution+-+CONS) by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies. Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030). In addition, Prop. 2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit (https://www.cde.ca.gov/fg/ac/gl/),” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong. The Legislature placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot through Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20).
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 2 would allow California to build a larger financial cushion by raising the maximum size of the state’s rainy day fund. It would also direct a greater share of unusually strong revenues into savings during high-revenue years. Having more money set aside could give the state greater flexibility during economic downturns or other periods when tax collections fall short of expectations.
Proposition 2 would extend requirements for additional state debt payments through 2040. As a result, California could pay down more of its outstanding debts and long-term financial obligations than it otherwise would under current rules.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s rainy day fund rules to allow larger reserves, increase deposits when revenues are strong, extend required debt payments through 2040, and change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending limit. It would also allow the governor’s May budget revision to serve as a declaration of a budget emergency when certain conditions are met.
NO: A “no” vote opposes these changes and would keep the current rules for the state’s rainy day fund, extra debt payments, spending limit, and declarations of budget emergencies.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 2 would strengthen California’s financial reserves by saving more during strong revenue years, helping the state avoid deep program cuts when the economy or tax revenues decline.

### Background
#### Reserves
***State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.”*** The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year.
Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program.
In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal.
During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
***Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level.*** Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits.
The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).

Proposition 2
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The deposits would not count toward the voter-approved Gann Limit, which caps the amount state lawmakers can spend each year and requires excess funds to be returned to the people. It also authorizes spending some tax revenue to pay down California’s $20 billion federal unemployment insurance debt. The California Legislature placed this measure on the ballot.

California’s tax revenue is volatile and relies heavily on the stock market. Supporters say raising the ceiling would allow the state to save more when the economy is booming, building a stronger reserve for economic downturns.

Additional details about our methodology can be found at www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/SurveyMethodology.pdf (http://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/SurveyMethodology.pdf) and are available upon request through [email protected] (https://www.ppic.org/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#7704020501120e043707071e1459180510).
Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). The DSF-based sampling frame used for address selection is enhanced with a series of refinements—such as the appendage of various ancillary data to each address from commercial and government data sources—to facilitate complex stratification plans. Taking advantage of such refinements, quarterly samples are selected using a stratified sampling methodology that aims to retain the representativeness of the panel. KnowledgePanel recruits new panel members throughout the year to offset panel attrition.
To qualify for the survey, a panel member must be age 18 or older and reside in California. A general population sample of Californians was selected using Ipsos’s PPS (probability proportional to size) sampling procedure to select study-specific samples. Briefly, to select such samples, the panel is first weighted to population benchmarks and those panel weights are used as the measure of size for a PPS sample selection that yields a fully representative sample. A total of 1,800 respondents completed the survey out of 3,046 panelists who were sampled, for a response rate of 59 percent. To ensure the highest data quality, we flagged respondents who sped through the survey, which we defined as completing the survey in one-fourth of the overall median time (less than 3.5 minutes). We also flagged respondents if their self-reported age or gender did not match the data stored in their profile. A total of 72 cases were removed after this review process, resulting in 1,728 total qualified and valid cases.
Accent on Languages, Inc., translated new survey questions into Spanish, with assistance from Renatta DeFever.
We use the US Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey’s (ACS) Public Use Microdata Series for California (with regional coding information from the University of Minnesota’s Integrated Public Use Microdata Series for California) to compare certain demographic characteristics of the survey sample—region, age, gender, race/ethnicity, education, and income—with the characteristics of California’s adult population. The survey sample was closely comparable to the ACS figures. We also used voter registration data from the California Secretary of State to compare the party registration of registered voters in our sample to party registration statewide. The sample of Californians is first weighted using an initial sampling or base weight that corrects for any differences in the probability of selecting various segments of the KnowledgePanel sample. This base weight is further adjusted using an iterative proportional fitting (raking) procedure that aligns sample demographics to population benchmarks from the 2024 ACS data as well as party registration benchmarks from the California Secretary of State’s voter registration file.
The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3 percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the total unweighted sample of 1,728 adults. This means that 95 times out of 100, the results will be within 3 percentage points of what they would be if all adults in California were interviewed. The sampling error for unweighted subgroups is larger: for the 1,449 registered voters, the sampling error is ±3.3 percent; for the 1,086 likely voters, it is ±3.8 percent. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording, question order, and survey timing.
We present results for five geographic regions, accounting for approximately 90 percent of the state population. “Central Valley” includes Butte, Colusa, El Dorado, Fresno, Glenn, Kern, Kings, Madera, Merced, Placer, Sacramento, San Joaquin, Shasta, Stanislaus, Sutter, Tehama, Tulare, Yolo, and Yuba Counties. “San Francisco Bay Area” includes Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Solano, and Sonoma Counties. “Los Angeles” refers to Los Angeles County, “Inland Empire” refers to Riverside and San Bernardino Counties, and “Orange/San Diego” refers to Orange and San Diego Counties. Residents of other geographic areas are included in the results reported for all adults, registered voters, and likely voters, but sample sizes for these less-populous areas are not large enough to report separately.
We present results for non-Hispanic whites, who account for 35 percent of the state’s adult population, and also for Latinos, who account for 38 percent of the state’s adult population and constitute one of the fastest-growing voter groups. We also present results for non-Hispanic Asian Americans, who make up about 17 percent of the state’s adult population, and non-Hispanic African Americans, who comprise about 5 percent. Results for other racial/ethnic groups—such as Native Americans—are included in the results reported for all adults, registered voters, and likely voters, but sample sizes are not large enough for separate analysis. Results for African American and Asian American likely voters are combined with those of other racial/ethnic groups because sample sizes for African American and Asian American likely voters are too small for separate analysis. We compare the opinions of those who report they are registered Democrats, registered Republicans, and decline-to-state or independent voters; the results for those who say they are registered to vote in other parties are not large enough for separate analysis. We also analyze the responses of likely voters—so designated per their responses to survey questions about voter registration, previous election participation, intentions to vote this year, attention to election news, and current interest in politics.
Sample sizes and margins of error for each subgroup are presented in the table below.
The percentages presented in the report tables and in the questionnaire may not add to 100 due to rounding.
We compare current PPIC Statewide Survey results to those in our earlier surveys and national surveys conducted by ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos, Reuters/Ipsos, and Pew Research Center. Numerous questions were adapted from national surveys by Pew Research Center and Reuters/Ipsos. Additional details about our methodology can be found at www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/SurveyMethodology.pdf (http://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/SurveyMethodology.pdf) and are available upon request through [email protected] (https://www.ppic.org/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#205355525645595360505049430e4f5247).

Advocates of Proposition 2 say they want to make it easier for state lawmakers to beef up the "rainy day" fund to help pay for long-term debt such as pension obligations. But the measure would actually make it easier to raid the fund to use for short-term, non-emergency spending. Above, lawmakers are shown at the state Capitol in June. (AP)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: October 2, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT

State lawmakers — the same ones who have been approving spending plans for years that the Legislative Analyst’s Office says have billions of dollars in structural deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5091) despite the California Constitution’s requirement that budgets must be balanced — want you to believe they’re actually conscientious fiscal stewards.
That’s why in 2014, they won approval of a ballot measure that was sold to voters with the claim that it would force the Legislature to set aside 1.5% of general fund revenue to beef up the state’s Budget Stabilization Account — a “rainy day” fund that could be used to pay for specific state debts, starting with unfunded pension and retirement health care obligations.
It would also divert even more money to the fund when capital-gains revenue was surging, a common event in the Golden State due to all the wealthy individuals in Silicon Valley with stock options they can cash in when times are good.
But there was a mammoth loophole: Required contributions to the fund could be reduced or suspended after the governor and a majority of the Legislature declared a “budget emergency.”
That’s exactly what has happened over and over again. “Emergencies” were declared the last three completed fiscal years even though revenue was surging.
Now state lawmakers are back with another sham. Placed directly on the ballot by the Legislature, Proposition 2 would amend the Budget Stabilization Account by lifting the cap on how much could be contributed to it — something voters are being told would strengthen the account.
But that is built on the myth that lawmakers want to contribute more. The measure’s fine print (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/26/proposition-2-isnt-about-saving-money-its-another-sacramento-shell-game/) shows its real goal: to make it even easier for the state to avoid paying down long-term unfunded obligations by allowing lawmakers to use new rainy day funds to repay recent “budget borrowing.”
No on Proposition 2. It’s another fake reform meant to make Californians think state lawmakers are actually serious about their responsibilities.
The U-T also opposes Proposition 37 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_37,_Second_Mortgage_Homebuyer_Program_and_Revenue_Bond_Initiative_(2026)), which is less cynical than Proposition 2 but is equally unlikely to live up to the promises made about it.
The measure authorizes the state to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a middle-class down payment assistance program for purchasing newly constructed homes. Backers say it is structured in a way that ensures private bond investors, not state taxpayers, are on the hook for paying back the borrowing.
Its key provision: Eligible buyers would have to be able to make a 3% cash down payment on a home, but they could secure a fixed-rate second mortgage covering up to 17% of the purchase price. This in theory eliminates the traditional expectation of a 20% down payment.
What it doesn’t do in the slightest is to address the biggest reason California has a massive housing crisis: shelter’s extreme cost. Including condos, the median home price in the state is $775,000 (https://www.noradarealestate.com/blog/california-housing-market/). Median household income is about $99,000, according to a recent Census Bureau report (https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/CA/BZA210223). Whether a home purchase involves borrowing 80% or 97% of the sale price, the great majority of families are not going to be able to pay the resulting mortgage or mortgages.
Proposition 37 advocates somehow think that allowing qualified state residents to borrow more is a magic solution to the affordability crisis. But a Zillow calculator shows that with the interest rates available in recent months, a household income of at least $265,000 per year is generally necessary to buy a $775,000 home with a 3% down payment in California. Proposition 37 doesn’t change this daunting picture at all.
There are practical ways that the state could bring down the cost of housing. Leaders could ignore turf-protecting construction trade unions and incentivize use of the sturdy, durable prefabricated homes that now have big market shares in Japan and Great Britain. They could ignore revenue-protecting trial lawyers and fix flawed state rules that incentivize lawsuits against condo builders.

2
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Summary
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters : CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents : None submitted
Money Raised
Chart depicts total fundraising by all committees primarily formed for and against Prop 2.Totals are updated daily with contributions from Power Search (http://powersearch.sos.ca.gov/) and adjustments from the most recent Political Reform Division analysis. (http://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/cal-access-resources/measure-contributions/methodology)

Contributions in earlier election cycles and contributions between allied committees are excluded. Yes on Prop 2
No contributions have been reported to the Yes on 2 campaign in the election cycle when it appeared on the ballot.
No on Prop 2
No contributions have been reported to the No on 2 campaign in the election cycle when it appeared on the ballot.
What your vote means
Yes
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
No
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
More on Proposition 2
For background on Proposition 2, an analysis by the legislative analyst, endorsements for and against the measure, and more...
Read the California Voter Information Guide (http://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/).
Arguments
Pro
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
Con
Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

content.text:
Yu (https://calmatters.org/author/yue-yu/)
Published October 23, 2026 at 2:39 PM PDT
Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.kpbs.org%2Fnews%2Fscience-technology%2F2026%2F10%2F23%2Fcalifornia-has-more-revenue-than-expected-thanks-to-ai-should-the-state-save-it&display=page)
WhatsApp (https://api.whatsapp.com/send?text=California%20has%20more%20revenue%20than%20expected%20thanks%20to%20AI.%20Should%20the%20state%20save%20it%3F%20-%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.kpbs.org%2Fnews%2Fscience-technology%2F2026%2F10%2F23%2Fcalifornia-has-more-revenue-than-expected-thanks-to-ai-should-the-state-save-it)
Email (mailto:?body=California%20has%20more%20revenue%20than%20expected%20thanks%20to%20AI.%20Should%20the%20state%20save%20it%3F%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.kpbs.org%2Fnews%2Fscience-technology%2F2026%2F10%2F23%2Fcalifornia-has-more-revenue-than-expected-thanks-to-ai-should-the-state-save-it%0A%0AProponents%20say%20Prop.%202%20would%20allow%20the%20state%20to%20shore%20up%20its%20reserves%20for%20an%20economic%20downturn.%20Critics%20say%20it%20would%20only%20allow%20state%20leaders%20to%20spend%20more%20in%20the%20future.)
Fred Greaves
/
CalMatters
Gov. Gavin Newsom presents his revised 2025-26 budget proposal in Sacramento on May 14, 2025.
This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/) . Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming?
The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%.
Advertisement
Become a KPBS sponsor (https://www.kpbs.org/corporate-sponsorship)
It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster.
Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy.
Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty.
Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce.
“It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure.
Advertisement
Become a KPBS sponsor (https://www.kpbs.org/corporate-sponsorship)
Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend.
“When they say we're here for fiscal responsibility, it's like the devil offering a Bible study. Don't buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican.
How long have we had a rainy day fund?
Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst.
In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund.
But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments.
In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it.
“When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform.
The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools.
Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years.
A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for.
Bigger reserve = more to spend?
Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending.
“The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.”
“Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”
In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times.
“I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.”

Voters face ballot full of traps, tricks and trillion-dollar stakes
Oct
15
2026
October 15, 2026
From left: Jill Replogle, Destiny Torres, Jon Gould and Michael Moodian.
Dean Jon Gould breaks it down at LAist cram session
By Mimi Ko Cruz (mailto:mkcruz@uci.edu)
Jon Gould broke it down for the Orange County voters who packed a Corona del Mar senior center on Oct. 13: the ballot is long, the propositions are complicated, some of them designed that way on purpose.
The dean of UC Irvine’s School of Social Ecology was a featured expert at the LAist Orange County Ballot Cram Session, a free event hosted by reporters Jill Replogle and Destiny Torres at the OASIS Senior Center. Gould and Michael Moodian of Chapman University walked the audience through 13 statewide propositions, two Board of Supervisors runoffs, and a ranked choice voting measure in Irvine — pulling no punches along the way.
Here is a rundown of the statewide measures:
Proposition 1 – Affordable Housing Bond , authorizes $11.25 billion in bonds for affordable housing, with $1.25 billion set aside for veterans. Gould called it “one of the most straightforward propositions on the ballot,” but cautioned that the veteran angle is somewhat overstated. “This is really less about veterans than it is about general affordable housing in California,” he said. Polling at around 55 percent.
Proposition 2 – Rainy Day Fund , would raise the cap on how much of the state’s general fund can be saved, from 10% to 20%. Gould noted it has unusual bipartisan support — Newsom and the legislative Democrats back it, but so does the Los Angeles Chamber of Commerce and firefighters. Polling at about 60%, which Gould said makes it likely to pass. When asked if it would ease the strain on local budgets, Gould was succinct: “No. Full stop.”
Proposition 3 – High Income Tax Rate Made Permanent , would make permanent the income tax surcharge on high earners — roughly those making more than $370,000 for single filers — that voters first passed in 2012 and extended in 2016. If it expires in 2031, the highest rate of 12.3% would drop to around 9%. About 89% of revenues go to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges. Polling at 58%. Replogle offered this context: “If this gets rejected and the tax rate goes back to what it was before 2012 for those highest income earners, someone who makes $3 million a year would be taxed at the same rate as somebody who makes $73,000 a year.”
Proposition 4 – Public Funding for Elections , would allow state and non-charter local governments to use taxpayer money to fund candidate campaigns, a system already in place in about five or six charter cities including Berkeley. Polling poorly — 42% in one survey, 35% in another. Gould said voters appear to be reacting viscerally: “Ugh, politicians, I don’t want to spend money on them.” Supported by the League of Women Voters and Common Cause but largely flying under the radar.
Proposition 5 – Recall Reform , would separate the question of recalling an official from the vote to replace them, requiring a special election for any successor. Gould traced the issue back to the Josh Newman and Gray Davis recalls, where replacement candidates won with as little as 30 to 33% of the vote. “I don’t see this winning,” Gould said. Not polling well, and opposed by the Republican Party.
Proposition 37 – Home Buyer Loan Assistance , a $25 billion revenue bond program offering middle-income buyers a fixed-rate second mortgage of up to 17% of a new home’s price, with buyers still required to put 3% down. The state would essentially act as a mortgage broker, Gould said. “People who want a house who can’t afford a house are not spending a whole lot of time asking about the geopolitical or larger economic issues. They’re asking, how can I afford a house?” Strongly backed by realtors and the construction industry. Polling well, with Gould calling it “probably passable,” though he noted buyers would be leveraged at 97% of their home's value.
Proposition 38 – Medical Research Bond , an $8.4 billion bond for cancer, Alzheimer’s, and other disease research. Half the money would go to a specific UCLA-affiliated institute backed by the proposition’s primary funder, Gary Michaelson, who has put in $43 million of the $51 million raised, Moodian said. Gould declined to comment directly, saying simply, “Since I am employed by the University of California, I’m going to say nothing.”
Proposition 39 – Voter ID , would require government-issued photo ID at the polls and the last four digits of an ID on mail-in ballots, and direct election officials to cross-check voter rolls with citizenship data. “There is simply no evidence anywhere in America of widespread voter fraud. There just isn’t,” Gould said, though he acknowledged a secondary argument, that showing ID adds a sense of civic integrity to voting. California-based pollsters show it failing by large margins; some out-of-state pollsters show it winning. Gould said it is one to watch on election night. Driven by the California Republican Party and opposed by Democrats.
Proposition 40 – One-Time Billionaire Tax , would impose a 5% tax on the assets — not income — of Californians with a net worth over $1 billion. Revenues would go primarily to healthcare, with some going to education and food assistance. Despite what would seem like a politically easy sell, it is currently polling below 50%. “This goes against everything I thought I knew about political science,” Gould said. “I thought voters would say, ‘Oh my God, we need money. It’s going to education. It’s going to healthcare. And it’s billionaires — sign me up.’ And, at the moment, it sure doesn’t look like that.” Supported by Senator Bernie Sanders; opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom and establishment Democrats.
Proposition 41 – Pre-Vote Tax Audit Requirement , would require the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. Gould said this is the most technically difficult proposition to understand, but the cleaner way to grasp it is this: a yes on 41 is effectively a no on Prop. 40, since it would nullify the billionaire tax if both pass. Funded heavily by billionaires opposing Prop. 40. Currently polling worse than Prop. 40 itself.
Proposition 42 – Ban on Personal Property Taxes , would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — not real estate — and ban retroactive taxes. Like Prop. 41, it is designed to undercut Prop. 40, and is heavily funded by tech billionaires including Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Gould noted that it has produced its own strange political coalition: technology investors and business groups are aligned with construction trade unions, firefighters and police, who are worried about retirement accounts. “If you are confused, that was intentional by the people who wrote 41 and 42, because they are trying to muddy the waters on 40.”
Proposition 43 – Two-Thirds Threshold for Local Special Taxes , would require a two-thirds voter approval for citizen-initiated local special taxes, up from a simple majority. Already failing badly in polling. Gould noted an irony: though it sounds like a citizen-led idea, it was placed on the ballot by the legislature in a deal to head off something more restrictive from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.
Proposition 44 – Community Clinic Spending Rule , would require nonprofit community health clinics to spend 90% of their revenues on direct patient care or face fines. Currently losing 2-to-1 in the only available poll.
Proposition 45 – CEQA Reform , would impose roughly a one-year deadline on environmental reviews and legal challenges for so-called essential projects including housing, roads, schools, broadband, and wildfire mitigation. Polling about 50-50. “If it weren’t for the housing crisis right now, I don’t think 45 would be on the ballot, and I don’t think it would pass,” Gould said. “But given the housing crisis that we’re having, this one’s really in play.” Supported by developers, utilities and the chambers of commerce; opposed by environmental groups and some labor unions.
Orange County Board of Supervisors races
On the Board of Supervisors, Gould called the District 5 race between incumbent Democrat Katrina Foley and former Newport Beach Mayor Diane Dixon “probably the most competitive of any of the races we are going to see in Orange County in 2026.”
He pointed to a notable wrinkle: outgoing Democratic supervisor Doug Chaffee has not endorsed Foley and is listed as a supporter on Dixon's website — a move Gould called “the controversy that is hiding in plain sight in this race.”
Foley has out-raised Dixon roughly 3 to 1, pulling in about $3 million largely from public employee and police and fire unions.
In District 4, which covers Brea, Fullerton, and parts of Anaheim, Democrat Connor Trout faces Republican Tim Shaw for the seat being vacated by Chaffee.
Democrats hold a roughly 10-point registration advantage in the district, though Gould cautioned that advantage has not always translated into wins.
Ranked choice voting
The panel closed with a discussion of an Irvine initiative to adopt ranked choice voting for city council and mayoral races — a measure endorsed by the Irvine mayor and opposed by the vice mayor. Gould said if it passes and voters embrace it, it could become a model for other California cities.
